APPENDIX.

THE ANNUAL COMMUNICATION OP THE EXECUTIVE
COUNCIL TO THE CONVENTION OF 1891.

I. New Chapters. The applications for Chapters at the Universities of

Pennsylvania and Minnesota were granted in April.
The petitioners from Pennsylvania having applied to the Fraternity to
be relieved from- the full performance of the conditions imposed by Gen.
Res. No. 11 of 1888, the application was referred to the Chapters by the
Council, and was speedily granted. The new Tau Chapter was accord
ingly initiated at Philadelphia on the evening of May 5, 1891, with thirtyfour charter members, including all members of the Upsilon Kappa Society
of the University of Pennsylvania, who have became associated with the
original petitioners since 1888. The Chapter occupies a comfortable and
handsomely equipped house in a most advantageous position at the inter
section of Thirty-sixth and Locust streets and Woodland avenue, Phila
delphia, opposite the main building of the University.
The petitioners from Minnesota will probably be initiated on or about
May 22d. They have proposed to assume the name of Theta Phi, from
the name of their provisional organization. The Chapter will have ninetyone charter members, some of whom, however, are already active mem

bers of the Fraternity, having passed from the University of Minnesota to

colleges represented in the Fraternity.
It is believed that the new Chapters, from the character of their mem
bership and of their Universities, as well as from the patience and persist
ence with which they have maintained the purpose of their organization

in spite of discouragement, display an inherent strength, which will make
them valuable additions to Psi Upsilon,
II. Applications for Charters. In accordance with the resolution of
the Convention of 1890, the Council appointed Daniel G. Thompson
(Gamma, '69), Robert Lenox Belknap (Lambda, '69), Frank L. Hall (Beta,
'71). a committee to inquire as to the advisability of establishing a Chapter
at Dickinson College, Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Their report is herewith sub
mitted.
An application for the establishment of a Chapter at the Massachusetts

12

Institute of Technology, Boston, Massachusetts, has been received by the
Council, and is herewith submitted with accompanying documents.
III. The Psi. Under General Resolution No. 10 of 1890, the Executive
Council by one of its members made a careful investigation of the affairs of
the Psi, They found that owing to the greatly increased interest on the
part of the graduate members of that Chapter a large part of the liabilities
of the Chapter had been paid ; that the perils which threatened the Chapter
at the time of the last Convention had been safely passed ; the prospects of
the Chapter were much brighter than they had been before in years ; the
Chapter house, with a few contemplated repairs and renovations, would
be very attractive ; and that with the confidently anticipated improvement
in the College itself the future of the Chapter would be fully assured.
The total unsecured balance of the liabilities of the Trustees of the Chapter
at the time of the report was but $1,100, and there was no danger that that
amount would not be raised as rapidly as required. The appointment of a
Committee to co operate with the active members of that Chapter was
therefore found unnecessary.
IV. Membebship. The active membership of the Fraternity on February
1, 1891, as reported, was 444, an increase of 33 over the membership of 1890-
V. The Tenth Oataloque. There has been a moderate demand for the

catalogue during the year. Three copies have been sold and two given
away, the latter having been taken from the number allotted to the editor
for exchange and complimentary distribution.
The Iota, Psi and Eta Chapters have accepted the terms for the settle
ment of their catalogue assessments prescribed by General Resolution No.
9 of 1890, and have paid their first installments. Credit has not been given
to the Psi in the Treasurer's statement, which necessarily went to press
before payment was made.
VI. New Song Book. The preparation of che manuscript of the
Song
Book is nearly completed and is partly in the hands of the printer. The
Council has employed Mr. H. P. Main, of New York, to assist Professor
Harrington, the editor, as an expert in the compilation of works of this
kind, particularly in regard to proof reading, copyrights and the prepara
tion and arrangement of the musical text. The Council is informed that
the book will doubtless be ready for delivery in September. The estimated
cost of an edition of 1,000 copies is about $1,725, details of which are here
with submitted Such an edition at a price of not less than $1.75
per copy
is recommended. An immediate sale of 450 copies at from $1,75 to
|8 per
copy will enable the Council, with other available funds in the Treasury, to
pay all bills without inconvenience ; but it is essential for this end that the
Chapters shall be prepared early in September without fail to take and pay
for the copies for which they have subscribed.
The Convention of 1890 required the Chapters to notify the Council
by
June 15, 1890, of the number of Song Books they would agree to take. No
response has yet been received from the Iota, Phi, Chi or Eta. Sub-

13

scriptions have been received, as follows : Theta, 31 ; Delta, 50 ; Beta, 15 ;
Sigma, 10 ; Ganpima, 30 ; Zeta, 15 ; Lambda, 30 ; Kappa, 85 ; Psi, 10 (at a
price not exceeding $1 each) ; Xi, 93 ; Upsilon, 15 ; Pi, 50 ; Beta Beta, 38 ;
total, 386.
VII. Finances. The Treasurer's report is hereto annexed. The treasury
has been in good condition, and the gradual accumulation of funds
during
preceding years enables the Fraternity to provide for the large
outlay now

required for the Song Book without an assessment or other extra demands
upon individual members or Chapters.
A tax of $1 per active member, to be applied to the general purposes of
the Fraternity, is recommended for the ensuing year.

Herbert L. Bridgman, President.
Benjamin H. Bayliss.
Henry C. Johnson.
